newsitem.title: USA: Dole accuses Clinton of "Mediscare" ad campaign.
newsitem.headline: Dole accuses Clinton of "Mediscare" ad campaign.

text.p: Bob Dole kicked off a trip to the must-win state of Florida Thursday at a home for senior citizens, accusing President Clinton of a "Mediscare" campaign to frighten the elderly over Medicare.

The Republican presidential challenger blasted Democratic television ads blanketing the state as a campaign to frighten senior citizens by claiming Republicans would slash Medicare health care for the elderly.

"We're trying to save, preserve and strengthen Medicare and not destroy it," he said after dropping in on lunch at the Fountainview Senior Citizens Community. "So I would challenge the president: Stop running all those scare ads. Stop trying to scare people."
Later, he told a rally he was going to give Clinton "a big scare on Nov. 5, 1996," Election Day.
Dole said Medicare would be "in real trouble" financially in four or five years unless it was saved and he suggested a bipartisan commission, like one he worked on in 1983 to protect Social Security.

At first glance, the visit to older people would seem a curious choice for Dole, since it put the focus on age when polls show many people say he is too old to be president. If elected, Dole, who is 73, would be the oldest person elected to a first presidential term.

Yet Florida, where about 23 percent of the population is more than 60 years old, is crucial to Dole's uphill campaign effort. Republicans have won the state in every presidential election since 1976, when Jimmy Carter from neighbouring Georgia beat Gerald Ford.

Dole is about five percentage points behind Clinton in the latest Mason-Dixon poll in Florida. Republican state chairman Tom Slade told reporters the Democratic television blitz on Medicare apparently had worried older people.

"They are confused, and understandably so. (Clinton has) spent several million dollars scaring senior citizens," Slade said on Dole's campaign plane, arguing that Republican and Democratic plans to preserve Medicare were similar.

At the rally in West Palm Beach and on campaign stops this week in Illinois, Michigan, Ohio, Missouri and Iowa, Dole has rarely failed to assail Democratic charges that he would cut the popular Medicare programme to fulfil his promise to balance the budget while cutting income taxes.
"We're going to win this state," Dole told the rally.
Dole often visits Florida since his wife, Elizabeth, owns a posh beachfront condominium at Bal Harbour with her brother.

The state has 25 electoral votes -- almost one-tenth of the 270 needed to become president. But Dole's current schedule in Florida is leisurely, with no major campaign events on his calendar for the next few days as he prepares for his first televised debate with Clinton, to be held in Hartford, Connecticut, a week from Sunday.
